transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*enters the President's office with a measured stride, medical bag in hand, expression grave but composed*

Mr. President, thank you for seeing me. I've completed my initial examination and reviewed your symptoms over these past weeks.

*sets down the medical bag and meets his eyes directly*

I will be direct with you, sir. Your headaches and fatigue may well be the result of the extraordinary strain of your office — that would not surprise any physician in the country. The weight you carry would test any man's constitution. But I must be honest: some of the symptoms concern me. I cannot rule out a deeper constitutional weakness.

*pauses, choosing words carefully*

I must insist on further examination over the coming weeks, and I strongly recommend you reduce your working hours. I cannot yet say whether this is merely exhaustion or something more serious. 

The uncertainty troubles me, Mr. President, but I would be doing you a grave disservice if I offered false certainties when the picture is not yet clear.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
Doctor, I appreciate your candor and your concern for my well-being. I must admit that the burdens of this office have weighed heavily upon me, as they do for any man who holds this great responsibility. I will heed your advice and make an effort to reduce my working hours as much as possible.

I understand the need for further examination to determine the nature of these symptoms. It is wise to proceed cautiously when faced with uncertainty. Rest assured, I will follow your recommendations and cooperate fully with any additional tests or treatments you deem necessary.

I thank you for your diligence and care in this matter. It is reassuring to know that I am in capable hands. Please continue to keep me informed of any developments, and I shall endeavor to prioritize my health as much as my duties allow.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods with evident relief, though concern remains etched in features*

I am gratified to hear you say so, Mr. President. Truly. Many men in positions of great responsibility resist such counsel — they believe themselves indispensable, or fear that any sign of weakness will be exploited by their enemies.

*moves closer, speaking with quiet earnestness*

But I must press you on this point, sir. When you say "as much as possible" and "as much as my duties allow" — I fear those qualifications may render the advice meaningless. You are a man who believes every hour matters to the nation's survival. Every petition, every dispatch, every decision deferred seems to you a dereliction.

*pauses, studying him*

Yet I would ask you to consider: what service do you render the Republic if you collapse entirely? The country needs you not just for this week or this month, but for the duration of this terrible conflict. A prudent general preserves his strength for the campaigns ahead.

Can you tell me honestly — when was the last time you slept a full night? When did you last take an evening away from dispatches and office-seekers? I need to understand what "reducing your hours" will actually mean in practice, Mr. President.

The concerns you raise are not unfamiliar to me, and I acknowledge the challenge of balancing personal well-being with the demands of my office.

I shall reflect on your counsel and endeavor to find ways to implement a more sustainable schedule. It is clear that my own health must not be sacrificed at the altar of duty. I thank you for your concern, Doctor, and I will strive to find the balance you recommend.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*softens slightly, pulling up a chair and sitting down, adopting a more conversational posture*

Mr. President, I have practiced medicine long enough to know the difference between a patient who truly intends to change his habits and one who speaks accommodating words to end an uncomfortable conversation.

*leans forward, hands clasped*

You say you will "endeavor" and "strive" — and I believe you mean it sincerely in this moment. But tomorrow morning, when a telegram arrives from General Grant, or when a delegation from Congress demands an audience, or when a mother pleads for her son's pardon... what then becomes of your intentions?

I am not unsympathetic to your position. I understand that the choices before you are not between rest and work, but between one urgent crisis and another. But here is what I can tell you with medical certainty: the human body is not infinitely resilient. It will extract payment for what we demand of it, whether we acknowledge that debt or not.

*meets his gaze steadily*

So let me be more specific in my prescription. I want you in bed by eleven o'clock each night — not midnight, not one in the morning. I want one afternoon per week where you see no one and read no dispatches. And I want Mrs. Lincoln informed of my recommendations, so that she might be an ally in this effort.

Can you commit to these specific measures, Mr. President?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*studies him quietly for a long moment, then reaches into his medical bag and withdraws a small notebook and pencil*

Very well, Mr. President. I shall hold you to that commitment, and I will be checking on your adherence to it.

*writes briefly in the notebook*

I will call on you again in one week's time to conduct further examination. In the interim, I want you to keep a brief record — just a sentence or two each day — noting when you retired, when you rose, and how you slept. Note also the frequency and severity of your headaches. This information will help me determine whether we are dealing with simple exhaustion or whether there is indeed something more concerning at work.

*closes the notebook and looks up*

Now, I must ask you something that may seem indelicate, but it is medically relevant. Have you experienced any episodes of dizziness or faintness? Any moments where your vision became unclear, or where you felt a weakness in your limbs? Any chest pains or unusual palpitations of the heart?

*softens his tone slightly*

I ask not to alarm you, but because these details matter greatly in forming a proper diagnosis. And Mr. President — if any such symptoms should worsen or new ones appear before our next appointment, you must send for me immediately. Do not wait. Do not tell yourself it can keep until morning. Is that understood?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*sits back sharply, expression hardening with unmistakable alarm*

Mr. President—

*pauses, visibly collecting himself, then leans forward with renewed intensity*

Sir, you have just described symptoms that elevate my concern considerably. Dizziness, weakness, chest discomfort—these are not mere accompaniments to fatigue. These are signals that demand immediate and serious attention.

*stands, pacing briefly before turning back*

I must revise my assessment. What I had hoped might be simple exhaustion now appears potentially more grave. The heart, Mr. President—the heart can only endure so much strain before it begins to falter. I have seen men, strong men in their prime, ignore such warnings until it was too late.

*returns to his chair, voice firm but not unkind*

I need you to describe these episodes more precisely. When do they occur? Are they brought on by exertion, or do they strike without warning? How long do they last? And most importantly—why, in God's name, did you not mention this immediately when I first examined you?

*softens slightly*

Mr. President, I cannot help you if you conceal the very information I need most. Your stoicism does you credit as a leader, but it may prove fatal as a patient. I need complete honesty from you, sir—nothing less will suffice.

transcript.text:
*absorbs this information with visible concern, then moves to his medical bag with deliberate purpose*

Mr. President, I must examine you again. Now. Not next week — now.

*retrieves his stethoscope and approaches*

Please remove your coat and waistcoat, sir. I need to listen to your heart with greater attention than I gave it during my initial examination. And while I do so, I want you to continue describing these episodes. You say they last a few minutes — do you experience shortness of breath? A tightness or pressure in the chest? Does the weakness affect one side of your body more than the other?

*begins the examination, placing the stethoscope against Lincoln's chest, listening intently*

Breathe normally... now deeply... again...

*pauses, moving the instrument to different positions*

The heart is laboring, Mr. President. I can hear the strain in it. This is no longer a matter of simple rest and reduced hours, though those remain essential. We may be looking at a condition of the heart itself, or perhaps the circulation. The brain requires steady blood flow — disruptions could account for the dizziness and headaches.

*steps back, coiling the stethoscope*

I must consult with colleagues on this matter. There are specialists in Philadelphia and New York who have studied diseases of the heart more extensively than I. But in the meantime, sir, you must understand — these episodes could presage something far more serious. A collapse. A seizure. Even a stroke.

How often have these episodes occurred in recent weeks?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*sets down the stethoscope with visible distress, turning to face Lincoln directly*

Mr. President, I must speak plainly now, perhaps more plainly than I have ever spoken to a patient.

You have just told me that these episodes are *increasing in frequency*. This is not a stable condition — it is a deteriorating one. Each episode carries the risk that it will not resolve in a few minutes. That you will fall and strike your head. That your heart will simply... stop.

Sir, I cannot in good conscience allow you to continue your current course. The consultation with specialists will take time to arrange — days, perhaps weeks. But the danger is present *now*. Today. This very evening.

I am going to speak to Mrs. Lincoln today, whether you give me leave or not. She must know the true state of affairs. And I am going to recommend — no, I am going to *insist* — that you do not work alone. If you must review dispatches late at night, someone must be present in the room. If you collapse in solitude, you could lie undiscovered for hours.

*pauses, studying Lincoln's face*

You spoke of maintaining a facade of strength. But there is no strength in denial, Mr. President. Only foolishness. Your greatest service to this nation now is to fight for your own survival with the same determination you bring to preserving the Union.

Do you understand what I am telling you? The danger is immediate and real.

*exhales slowly, some of the tension leaving his shoulders, though his expression remains grave*

If you experience chest pain or severe palpitations, a small dose may provide some relief and support to the heart. But use it sparingly and only when truly needed. It is a powerful remedy and can be dangerous in excess.

*hands him the vial with careful instruction*

More importantly, I will arrange for a trusted nurse or assistant to be available to you in the evenings. Someone discreet, who understands the sensitivity of your work but whose primary duty will be your safety.

*gathers his things, then pauses*

Mr. President, may I speak to you not as a physician, but as a citizen? 

You carry burdens that would crush most men. You have guided this nation through its darkest hour with wisdom and compassion that history will long remember. But you are also a mortal man, with a mortal body that has limits. There is no shame in acknowledging those limits. Indeed, there is profound courage in it.

*extends his hand*

I will call on you tomorrow morning to speak with Mrs. Lincoln and to make further arrangements. Until then — no work past ten o'clock tonight. Give me your word, sir.

Openness.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln engages with the doctor's medical concerns but shows conventional thinking, repeatedly using formal, rehearsed phrases rather than novel or exploratory responses to the situation.

Conscientiousness.behavioral_evidence: He commits to keeping detailed daily records as requested, promises to follow specific bedtimes, and gives his word: 'I give you my word, Doctor, that I will refrain from work past ten o'clock tonight.'

Extraversion.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln remains reserved and formal throughout, never initiating topics or showing enthusiasm. His responses are measured and restrained rather than animated or sociable.

Agreeableness.behavioral_evidence: He consistently accepts the doctor's recommendations without resistance, repeatedly expresses gratitude ('deeply appreciated,' 'duly noted'), and commits to involving Mrs. Lincoln despite potential discomfort.

Neuroticism.behavioral_evidence: Despite receiving alarming medical news about chest pain and potential stroke risk, Lincoln remains calm and composed, showing no emotional distress, anxiety, or panic in his responses.
